summary_html: An intake **screen** is elevated to a formal **investigation/assessment** under state criteria. CAPTA and CFSR establish the federal expectations for screening, timelines, and investigative quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening/investigation conditions for funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review framework

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Owen v. Missouri Department of Social Services, Children's Division
key_cases.holding: The court reversed and remanded, holding that the Children's Division has statutory authority to investigate and to list on the Central Registry a non-resident who abused a Missouri child outside Missouri, and describing the hotline-to-investigation-to-registry sequence set by sections 210.145 and 210.152.
key_cases.relevance: The case turns on the Division's authority to escalate a screened report into a formal investigation and a registry listing.
key_cases.quote: The circuit court erred as a matter of law in concluding that the Children's Division lacked authority to investigate Owen's out-of-state abuse of a Missouri minor child

key_cases.case_name: C.S. v. Missouri Department of Social Services, Children's Division
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the judgment upholding the Central Registry listing, holding that Chapter 210 does not confine the circuit court's de novo review to the specific allegations set out in the Division's notice of substantiated findings and that admitting additional evidence did not violate due process.
key_cases.relevance: The decision shows how allegations that surface after the initial screening can still be litigated once the investigation has escalated to a substantiated finding.
key_cases.quote: Chapter 210 does not limit a circuit court's de novo review to allegations of specific misconduct set out in the Division's Notice of Substantiated Findings

key_cases.case_name: C.D.J., Jr. v. Missouri Department of Social Services, Children's Division
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that a family whose child is recorded as abused has standing to seek review and that the Children's Division lacks statutory authority to substantiate a report of abuse by an 'unknown perpetrator.'
key_cases.relevance: The opinion traces the escalation from report to investigation and the limits on what the Division may record at the end of it.
key_cases.quote: the Children's Division does not have the statutory authority to substantiate a report that an "unknown perpetrator" committed child abuse

key_cases.case_name: Jamison v. State, Department of Social Services, Division of Family Services
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed in part and reversed in part, holding that a person faces a protected liberty interest in not being listed on the Central Registry, that due process therefore requires notice and a pre-deprivation CANRB hearing applying a preponderance of the evidence standard before listing, and that the same preponderance standard governs de novo judicial review of a CANRB decision.
key_cases.relevance: The decision governs the moment a screened report escalates into a substantiated determination with legal consequences, and holds an investigator's or local director's finding cannot alone carry that escalation.
key_cases.quote: Unless and until the CANRB determines that the allegations are proven by a preponderance of the evidence, the division cannot constitutionally include the alleged perpetrators in the Central Registry.

state_agency.name: Missouri Department of Social Services, Children's Division

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, medical examiners, coroners, dentists, chiropractors, optometrists, podiatrists, residents, interns, nurses, hospital or clinic personnel, and any other health practitioner — Mo. Rev. Stat. § 210.115.1
Psychologists, mental health professionals, and social workers
Day care center workers and other child-care workers
Juvenile officers, probation or parole officers
Teachers, principals, and other school officials
Ministers, as provided by Mo. Rev. Stat. § 352.400
Peace officers and law enforcement officials
Volunteers or personnel of a community service program that offers support services for families in crisis (Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 475.600 to 475.604)
Any other person with responsibility for the care of children
reporting_details: Missouri is not a universal-reporter state — the professionals and officials listed in Mo. Rev. Stat. § 210.115.1 must immediately report suspected abuse or neglect to the Children's Division and violating that duty is a class A misdemeanor (§ 210.165.1), while any other person may report voluntarily under § 210.115.5.

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours to initiate the investigation or family assessment (72 hours if educational neglect is the only complaint); direct observation of the child within 24 hours if the report indicates danger of serious physical harm or threat to life
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the report by the division
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Mo. Rev. Stat. § 210.145.

timeline_requirements.deadline: 45 days; extendable only for good cause specifically documented, and no later than 90 days (120 days for reports involving sexual abuse, or until complete for a child fatality or near-fatality)
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the report of abuse or neglect
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Good cause for not completing within 45 days must be specifically documented in the information system, which must then be updated at regular intervals until the investigation is complete (Mo. Rev. Stat. § 210.145.17(1), (3)).
